title: Ring strain: angle strain, torsional strain and the numbers
asks: Compare cycloalkanes: where the strain comes from, how many eclipsing interactions, which ring is most stable and why.

know.h: Ring strain has two parts: 1. angle strain (C-C-C angles forced away from the tetrahedral 109.5°) and 2. torsional strain (eclipsed C-H bonds on neighbouring carbons).
Angles to know: cyclopropane 60°; flat cyclobutane 90° (puckered, 88°); flat cyclopentane 108°; flat cyclohexane 120°; chair cyclohexane 111.5°.
A flat ring of n carbons has 2n eclipsing C-H/C-H interactions: cyclopropane 6, cyclobutane 8, cyclopentane 10, cyclohexane 12.

Bent bonds: in cyclopropane the {{sp3}} orbitals cannot point along the lines between the carbons, so they overlap off the axis. Less overlap means a weaker bond: C-C is 65 kcal/mol in cyclopropane against 88 in propane.

Rings pucker to relieve torsional strain. Cyclobutane puckers (relieves some torsional strain; the angle goes from 90° to 88°). Cyclopentane has two puckered energy minima: lots of torsional strain relieved, at the expense of angle strain.
The chair of cyclohexane has no angle strain and no torsional strain: all carbons are tetrahedral and all C-H bonds on adjacent carbons are staggered.
Heats of formation per {{CH2}}, kcal/mol: cyclopropane +4.2; cyclobutane +1.7; cyclopentane -3.7; cyclohexane -4.9 (most stable); cycloheptane -4.0; strain-free chain -4.9.

Strain per {{CH2}} is the heat of formation per {{CH2}} minus the strain-free value (-4.9). Multiply by the number of {{CH2}} groups for the whole ring: cyclopropane 3 x 9.1 = 27.3; cyclobutane 4 x 6.6 = 26.4; cyclohexane 0.
A chair has six axial hydrogens (vertical) and six equatorial hydrogens (around the middle). The ring flip swaps them, and for cyclohexane itself K = 1.
Axial groups cost energy. An axial methyl is gauche to two ring carbons (C3 and C5), like gauche butane twice. An equatorial methyl is anti to both, like anti butane.
Cost of an axial group and K: methyl 1.74 kcal/mol (K = 19.5); ethyl 1.79 (21.2); propyl 2.21 (43.4); isopropyl 2.61 (86.0); tert-butyl 5.5 (11,916).
K is the ratio of equatorial to axial molecules. The fraction equatorial is K / (K + 1): for methyl, 19.5 / 20.5 = 95%.
Skill: be able to draw a Newman projection down a ring bond and say whether two groups are eclipsed, gauche or anti.

method: Decide which kind of strain the question is about: angles (angle strain) or eclipsed bonds (torsional strain). Many rings have both.
For angle strain, compare the ring's angle with 109.5°.
For torsional strain in a flat ring, count 2 eclipsing C-H/C-H interactions per ring bond.
If the ring is puckered, say what it gains (less torsional strain) and what it pays (angle strain).
For stability, use the heat of formation per {{CH2}}: more negative is more stable, and -4.9 means strain free.
For a substituted chair, count axial groups and use Table 5.3 for the cost and K.

pitfalls.h: Saying a ring has only angle strain. Flat rings also have eclipsed hydrogens, and in cyclopentane torsional strain is the main problem.
Saying puckering fixes the angles. Puckering relieves torsional strain and costs some angle strain.
Mixing up per {{CH2}} and per molecule, or reading a heat of formation as the strain. Strain is measured from -4.9 per {{CH2}}.
Assuming bigger rings are always more stable. Cycloheptane (-4.0) is less stable per {{CH2}} than cyclohexane (-4.9).
Reading K as an energy, or a large K as proof that the ring cannot flip.
